Acceleration of a [[Chemical reaction|chemical reaction]] by an added substance, the catalyst, that is not consumed and remains unchanged afterward. It works by opening an alternative mechanism with a lower activation energy, which may be much faster than the uncatalyzed route. Because the uncatalyzed route remains possible, a catalyst can only increase the total rate, never decrease it. A catalyst has no effect on the [[Chemical equilibrium|chemical equilibrium]] of a reaction: one that shifted an equilibrium would amount to a perpetual motion machine, contradicting the [[Second law of thermodynamics]].

Catalysis is classed as homogeneous, when the catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants (usually gaseous or liquid), or heterogeneous, when it is not, as with a solid surface acting on gases or liquids. [[Enzyme|Enzymes]] and other biocatalysts are often considered a third category. Manganese dioxide speeds the decomposition of [[Hydrogen peroxide|hydrogen peroxide]] into water and oxygen (2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂); in living organisms the enzyme catalase does the same work. [[Nitric oxide]] catalyzes the oxidation of sulfur dioxide (2 SO₂ + O₂ → 2 SO₃). Platinum in [[Catalytic converter|catalytic converters]] helps purify exhaust gas.

The SI derived unit of catalytic activity is the katal, measured in moles per second. Estimates hold that 90% of all commercially produced chemical products involve catalysts at some stage of manufacture. The term derives from the Greek *kataluein*, 'loosen' or 'untie'; Jöns Jacob Berzelius is credited with coining it in 1835.

German-born empress of Russia (r. 1762–96). She married Peter, a grandson of [[Peter the Great]], at the age of 16. When he became emperor as Peter III in 1762, she overthrew him in a [[Coup d'état|coup]] after a brief reign, and ruled for more than 34 years.

Her reign was a period of rapid expansion by conquest and diplomacy. Victories over the [[Ottoman Empire]] in the Russo-Turkish War led to the annexation of the [[Crimean Khanate]] and to Russian colonization of New Russia along the Black and Azov seas. In the west, she installed her former lover on the throne of Poland, which was eventually partitioned (see [[Partitions of Poland]]). Russians also became the first Europeans to colonize Alaska.

She is often counted among the enlightened despots and corresponded with [[Voltaire]]; her Nakaz, a proposed legal instruction, drew on [[Montesquieu]]. She established the Smolny Institute of Noble Maidens, the first state-financed higher education institution for women in Europe; and founded the Imperial Public Library in 1795, which opened to the public in 1814. In 1783 she appointed Princess Yekaterina Dashkova director of the Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences, the first woman to head a national academy of sciences. She promoted [[Smallpox|smallpox]] inoculation, undergoing it herself in 1768.

Absolute monarchy persisted, and conscription and the economy continued to depend on serfdom, whose burdens intensified; this was among the chief causes of rebellions, including Pugachev's Rebellion. She was the first Russian ruler to bring abolition of serfdom into public debate, but enacted only measures restricting its expansion.

Largest Christian church, with an estimated 1.28 to 1.41 billion baptized members worldwide. It consists of 24 autonomous (*sui iuris*) churches: the Latin Church, the largest, and 23 smaller [[Eastern Catholic Churches]]. Together they are organized into nearly 3,500 dioceses and eparchies governed by bishops.

Doctrine is rooted in the [[Nicene Creed]] and holds that the church, founded by [[Jesus|Jesus Christ]], is the 'one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.' Bishops are held to be successors of the apostles, and the [[Pope|pope]], the bishop of Rome, successor of [[Saint Peter]]. The [[Holy See]] serves as the central governing authority through the Roman Curia.

The church observes seven sacraments, of which the [[Eucharist]], celebrated in the Mass, is regarded as the source and summit of Christian life. Catholics believe that through consecration by a priest the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Catholic social teaching emphasizes care for the poor, the sick, and the marginalized, and the church operates tens of thousands of educational, medical, and charitable institutions.

Schisms occurred with the Church of the East after the Council of Ephesus (431), with the Oriental Orthodox Churches after the Council of Chalcedon (451), and with the Eastern Orthodox churches. The 16th-century [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]] produced new Christian traditions. Since the late 20th century the church has faced criticism of its teachings on sexuality, clerical celibacy, and the ordination of women, and of its handling of clerical sexual abuse.

Large, domesticated, cloven-hooved bovid [[Ungulate|ungulates]] (*Bos taurus*) widely kept as [[Livestock|livestock]]. They are the most widespread species of the genus *Bos*. Taurine cattle are distributed across Europe and temperate Asia, the Americas, and Australia; zebus are found mainly in India and tropical areas; and sanga cattle occur primarily in sub-Saharan Africa. These types, sometimes classified as separate species or subspecies, are divided into over 1,000 recognized breeds.

Cattle are raised for meat, dairy products, and leather, and as draft animals they pull carts and farm implements. They are considered sacred in [[Hinduism]], and killing them is illegal in some parts of the Indian subcontinent. About 10,500 years ago, taurine cattle were domesticated from wild [[Aurochs|aurochs]] in central Anatolia, the Levant, and western Iran; a separate domestication in the Indian subcontinent gave rise to zebu.

Cattle are large artiodactyls that walk on two toes. Hereford bulls weigh 1,000–1,200 kg; the Chianina is the tallest and heaviest breed, with mature bulls reaching 1,280 kg. The natural life span is some 25–30 years. Beef cattle go to slaughter at about 18 months, and dairy cows at about five years.

Cattle are [[Ruminant|ruminants]], with a stomach of four compartments (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum). Bacteria, fungi, and protozoa in the rumen produce [[Enzyme|enzymes]] that split [[Cellulose|cellulose]] in grass into sugars. Food is regurgitated and re-chewed as cud. Gestation lasts about nine months, and calves are weaned at 8 to 11 months under natural conditions. Cattle farming is responsible for about 7% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Basic structural and functional unit of all forms of life. The term comes from the Latin *cellula*, 'small room'. A biological cell consists of a semipermeable [[Cell membrane|cell membrane]] enclosing [[Cytoplasm|cytoplasm]] that contains genetic material. Most cells are visible only under a [[Microscope|microscope]]. Except for highly differentiated types such as [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]] and gametes, most cells can replicate and synthesize protein, and some are motile. Cells emerged on Earth about four billion years ago.

Cells were discovered by [[Robert Hooke]] in 1665, who named them for their resemblance to the cells of a monastery. Cell theory, developed through the work of Matthias Jakob Schleiden in 1838 and Theodor Schwann in 1839, established the cell as the basic structural unit of plants and animals. It states that all organisms are composed of one or more cells, that cells are the fundamental unit of structure and function, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells.

All organisms are grouped into prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Prokaryotes, which include [[Archaea|archaea]] and [[Bacteria|bacteria]], are single-celled and lack a membrane-bound nucleus, having a nucleoid region instead. Most are the smallest of all organisms, 0.1 to 5.0 μm in diameter; the largest known bacterium, *Thiomargarita magnifica*, averages 1 cm in length and can reach 2 cm. A bacterial cell is enclosed in an envelope, typically a plasma membrane covered by a cell wall of peptidoglycan. Its DNA usually forms a single circular chromosome, and extra genes, such as those for antibiotic resistance, may sit on circular plasmids. Archaea have unique ether-linked membrane lipids, a form of metabolism called methanogenesis, and many extremophile species that thrive in extreme heat, cold, acidity, alkalinity, or salt. No archaean pathogens are known.

Eukaryotes can be single-celled, as in diatoms, yeasts, and some algae, or multicellular, as in animals, plants, most fungi, and seaweed. Their cells can be 2 to 100 times larger in diameter than a typical prokaryotic cell and have a membrane-bound nucleus, the largest organelle. Other organelles present in all eukaryotic cells include the endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, the Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes, peroxisomes, endosomes, and vesicles. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts, which make sugars by photosynthesis. The diploid cells that form the body of an animal or plant are called somatic cells, which excludes the haploid gametes.

Subregion of North America, an isthmus bordering Mexico to the north, Colombia to the southeast, the Caribbean to the east, and the Pacific Ocean to the southwest. It is usually defined as seven countries: Belize, [[Costa Rica]], [[El Salvador]], [[Guatemala]], [[Honduras]], [[Nicaragua]], and [[Panama]]; in specialized contexts Mexico is also included. The Mesoamerican biodiversity hotspot extends from southern Mexico to southeastern Panama. Active faults and the Central America Volcanic Arc make seismic activity high.

The region includes parts of two cultural areas: the Mesoamerican, covering Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador, and western Honduras and Nicaragua, and the Isthmo-Colombian, covering Panama, Costa Rica, and eastern Honduras and Nicaragua. Hundreds of indigenous groups lived there before the voyages of [[Christopher Columbus]], notably the Maya in the north. Spain began colonization from 1502 and began conquering the Maya kingdoms in 1523. From 1609 to 1821 most territories, except what became Belize and Panama, were governed from Mexico City as the Captaincy General of Guatemala within [[New Spain]].

Independence from Spain was proclaimed on September 15, 1821. Some provinces were annexed to the First Mexican Empire, but in 1823 they seceded to form the Federal Republic of Central America. Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua became independent countries in 1838, El Salvador in 1841, Panama in 1903, and Belize in 1981.

Economies depend heavily on agriculture, particularly coffee, bananas, and sugar, as well as tourism, manufacturing, and remittances from migrants in the United States. The Panama Canal opened in 1914. The region continues to face poverty, violence, corruption, and natural disasters.

Grass of the family [[Poaceae]] cultivated for its edible grain. Cereals are the world's largest crops and staple foods. They include [[Rice|rice]], [[Wheat|wheat]], rye, oats, barley, millet, and [[Maize|maize]] (U.S.: corn). Edible grains of other plant families, such as amaranth, buckwheat, and quinoa, are called pseudocereals. The term derives from Latin *cerealis*, 'of [the goddess] Ceres', the Roman deity of grain crops and fertility.

Botanically, a cereal grain is a caryopsis, a fruit in which the seed coat is fused with the pericarp. Most cereals are annuals harvested once after sowing; rice, usually treated as an annual, can survive as a perennial. Cool-season cereals such as barley, oats, rye, and wheat suit a [[Temperate climate|temperate climate]], while millet and sorghum prefer a tropical one.

Charred wild wheat and barley 19,000 years old have been found at Ohalo II in Israel. Cereals were domesticated in the [[Neolithic]] around 8,000 years ago: wheat and barley in the [[Fertile Crescent]], rice and some millets in East Asia, and sorghum and other millets in Sudan. Maize was domesticated by Indigenous peoples in Mexico about 9,000 years ago.

Between 1964 and 2023 cereal production increased by 213%, mostly through higher yields, as harvested area rose by only 10%. This followed the [[Green Revolution]], which relied on mechanized tilling, monoculture, nitrogen fertilizers, and new seed strains. Cereals are eaten as whole grains or ground to flour for bread, porridge, and other foods, and their starch can be fermented into beer. Cereal farming has a substantial environmental impact; no-till farming and intercropping can mitigate it.

King of the Franks (r. 768–814), King of the Lombards from 774, and first emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 800. He united most of Western and Central Europe and was the first recognized emperor to rule from the west since the fall of the Western Roman Empire about three centuries earlier.

The eldest son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon, he became king of the [[Franks]] in 768 with his brother Carloman I and sole ruler three years later. Continuing his father's policy, he became the chief defender of the papacy and ended Lombard rule in northern Italy in 774. His campaigns brought Bavaria, Saxony, and northern Spain under his rule. He spread Christianity into conquered lands, sometimes by force: the Saxon Wars involved mass executions, including the Massacre of Verden, and forced baptisms.

On Christmas Day 800 he was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III. Historians debate the coronation's significance, but it brought him into conflict with the Eastern Roman Empire in [[Constantinople]], and he is considered the forerunner of the Holy Roman Emperors. He carried out reforms in administration, law, education, military organization, and religion. His reign began a period of cultural activity known as the Carolingian Renaissance.

He died in 814 and was buried in the Palatine Chapel, now part of Aachen Cathedral, in [[Aachen]], his imperial capital. His empire fragmented after his death among his heirs. Many historians call him the 'Father of Europe,' and several European states and royal houses claim him as a founding figure.

English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, known for establishing the theory of [[Evolution|evolution]] by [[Natural selection|natural selection]]. He was honored by burial in [[Westminster Abbey]].

Born in Shrewsbury, Shropshire, he neglected his medical studies at the University of Edinburgh. At the [[University of Cambridge]]'s Christ's College (1828–31) his passion for natural science grew. His five-year voyage on HMS *Beagle* (1831–36) established him as an eminent geologist; his observations supported [[Charles Lyell]]'s concept of gradual geological change. His travel journal, *The Voyage of the Beagle* (1839), made him a popular author, and *The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs* (1842) was his first scientific work. Together with his work on barnacles, it won him the Royal Medal in 1853.

Puzzled by the distribution of the wildlife and fossils he had collected, he devised his theory of natural selection in 1838. In 1858, while he was writing it up, [[Alfred Russel Wallace]] sent him an essay outlining the same idea, prompting a joint presentation to the Linnean Society of London. Darwin set out his evidence in *[[On the Origin of Species]]* (1859). Later books included *Fertilisation of Orchids* (1862), *The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex* (1871), and *The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals* (1872).

By the 1870s the scientific community and a majority of the educated public had accepted evolution, though many favored explanations giving natural selection only a minor role. Broad consensus on natural selection as the basic mechanism came with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s to the 1950s.

English comic actor, filmmaker, singer, film editor, and composer of the silent-film era, creator of the screen persona the Tramp.

Chaplin's London childhood was one of poverty: his father was absent, and he was sent to a workhouse twice before the age of nine. At 14 his mother was committed to a mental asylum. He began performing early and at 19 was signed by the Fred Karno company, which took him to the United States. In 1914 he gained wide popularity in films for Keystone Studios and soon adopted the Tramp persona. By 1918 he was one of the world's best-paid and best-known figures.

In 1919 he co-founded the distribution company United Artists, giving him full control over his films. His features include *The Kid* (1921), *A Woman of Paris* (1923), *The Gold Rush* (1925), and *The Circus* (1928). He resisted sound films in the 1930s, producing [[City Lights]] (1931) and *Modern Times* (1936) without dialogue; his first sound film, *The Great Dictator* (1940), satirized [[Adolf Hitler]]. He wrote, directed, produced, edited, and composed the music for most of his films. His work combines slapstick with pathos, and many films contain social and political themes.

His popularity declined in the 1940s. He was accused of communist sympathies, and a paternity suit and his marriages to much younger women scandalized some of the press and public. The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] opened an investigation, and in 1952 he left the U.S. and settled in Switzerland. He abandoned the Tramp in later films such as *Limelight* (1952). He received an Honorary Academy Award in 1972 and a knighthood in 1975.
